title: Book: Stocks for the Long Run — Jeremy Siegel (1994)
publisher: Artha Kavach original summary of a book's ideas (paraphrase, not a quotation; the author's opinion, not settled fact) — pending manual verification
text: Jeremy Siegel uses very long US historical data to argue that, over long holding periods, a diversified portfolio of stocks has beaten bonds, gold and cash after inflation, even though stocks can fall sharply in any one year. The takeaway is that time in the market and a long horizon reduce the odds of losing money in equities and that holding safe assets for decades has its own inflation risk. Cautions: the evidence is mostly US data from a very successful market, past returns are not a promise, other countries have had long poor stretches, and people must be able to ride out large drawdowns. For goals under five years, the book's logic does not apply.
